newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bayer says no near-term acquisition planned.
newsitem.headline: Bayer says no near-term acquisition planned.

text.p: German chemical and drugs group Bayer AG on Thursday said it was not planning to make a big acquisition in the near term and similarly had no concrete plans to spin off its health care unit into a separate entity.

"We are not in favour of mega-acquisitions or mega- mergers...we can be successful in the present structure we have," Bayer chief financial officer Helmut Loehr told Reuters Financial Television in an interview broadcast on Thursday.

Only months after triggering market speculation that Bayer might plan to spin off its drugs unit into a separate legal entity and then possibly merge with another company, Loehr said Bayer was happy growing through its own strength.
Referring to the possibility of a spin-off, Loehr said, "This is a model or scenario which we have available in case a major merger would be possible."
But "for the time being, we will concentrate on exploiting our promising pipeline and strengthening our healthcare business from internal sources," he added.

One reason Loehr said Bayer was currently not electing to pursue the option of spinning off the drugs unit was that such a step would cost the group some 10 billion marks ($6.6 billion) in tax liabilities, a Bayer spokesman added.
Similarly Loehr shrugged off persistent market speculation that Bayer may be interested in making a bid for UK drugs group Zeneca Plc, which last week sent Zeneca shares to a new year high.

Responding to the question of whether Bayer was interested in buying Zeneca, with a current price tag said to be around $30 billion, Loehr said, "I would rule out any acquisition of this size due to the question of financing."
He added that prices for drugs companies, at a time when the entire industry was going through considerable reshaping, were "much too high."
If Bayer were to consider a merger in the health care sector, Loehr again said the group would want to retain a majority stake.
"However the result must be that we maintain control over the healthcare business of this merged company,"
While Bayer shares have been consistently strong since Loehr first raised the issue of a possible spin-off of the drugs unit, he predicted his group's share price had more potential to climb.
"The market still does not fully reflect what is possible for a diversified company," he said.
Loehr added that Bayer planned to convince the market of its strengths with a "good performance", sticking to the group's forecast of a 10 percent increase in 1996 pre-tax profits.
"The business up until now is in line with this forecast and I don't see any major problems but also no major potential for further improvement."
